The Sūtra says: "From here, passing through a hundred trillion Buddha-lands to the west, there is a world named Sukhāvatī.
It is adorned with the seven treasures; it has no three evil realms, nor are there women. Food and clothing appear spontaneously, and lifespans are immeasurable.
That Buddha is named Amitābha; he emits great radiance to receive and guide all sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha, so that they may be reborn there."
In that land, one is born by transformation from a lotus flower rather than through a womb.

If a person can single-mindedly take refuge in Amitābha Buddha, joining their palms daily toward the west and exclusively reciting the Buddha’s name—whether ten thousand times, ten thousand times, a thousand or hundred times, or even just ten recitations at the moment of death—they shall all attain rebirth there.
They will behold the Buddha, hear the Dharma, and never again fall back.
Those who are literate and able to read characters should recite one scroll, or three scrolls, of the Shorter Amitābha Sūtra every day, according to their strength and capacity;
they should also concurrently recite the Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra, the Meditation Sūtra, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, the Lotus Sūtra, the Complete Enlightenment Sūtra, and the Diamond Sūtra.

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, and other scriptures, as well as treatises such as the *Awakening of Faith* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, all constitute superior provisions for the path.

Furthermore, in daily life, one must receive and uphold the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, accumulate various merits, and dedicate them toward the Western Pure Land; in this way, the resulting efficacy will be more stable.
To claim that the place where Śākyamuni Buddha was born is the Western Pure Land is an error.
Śākyamuni was born in India (Tianzhu), which, like this land of China (Zhen dan), is situated within Jambudvīpa. It is a distance reachable by a single step.
These four great continents together constitute one set of four world-systems (*cāturdvīpaka*). One hundred billion such sets of four world-systems are called... [a *trichiliocosm*].
It constitutes a single buddha-field. From here, traveling westward across a hundred trillion buddha-fields, one reaches the world of Ultimate Bliss.
By this analogy, how could the distance between them be anything less than as vast as that between heaven and abyss?
The Tathāgata appears in the world for the sake of one great cause and condition: nothing other than to teach people to recognize their own fundamental mind and clearly perceive Buddha-nature.
This mind is the Buddha; apart from this mind, there is no Buddha. If one realizes this, one does not need to traverse the long journey.
One proceeds directly toward the place of treasure; this is called mindfulness of the Buddha of intrinsic nature, and it is also called mindfulness of the Buddha of true reality (*dharmatā*).

However, the faculties and capacities of these sentient beings are not uniform, making sudden entry into realization difficult. Even if one relies on the teachings to give rise to faith and personally accepts the responsibility, ignorance remains unbroken and the seeds of karma persist as before.
When entering or emerging from the womb, they lose their right mindfulness, leaving them utterly helpless. Regarding this...
Furthermore, he opened another gate for rebirth in the Pure Land, instructing practitioners to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha and dedicate their merit toward the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss;
this was because during the causal stage of his past lives, Amitābha Buddha had made forty-eight vows to universally encompass all classes of beings.
Whether wise or foolish, virtuous or evil, if one accomplishes the merit of ten recitations, one will cross over birth and death horizontally;
therefore, this is called the most supreme among all skillful means. To enter this gate, one must first understand suffering; once suffering is understood, [one proceeds].
One must seek to emerge from suffering. All sentient beings take suffering to be pleasure;

they do not reflect that this body, having existed for immeasurable kalpas, dwells but briefly among humans and devas, as fleeting as a flash of lightning. In an instant, one may wander through the hells upon copper pillars and iron beds;

The cycle of rebirth turns without end. Having now temporarily obtained this human life, aging, illness, death, and decline are as swift as a breath.
This foul impurity is no different from a stinking corpse. Is this not enough to arouse a resolute mind and give rise to diligent practice? By what means can one escape [suffering]?

He can bestow upon me official rank and provide for my food and clothing, yet he cannot release me from the wheel of suffering or open for me the gate of Right Enlightenment.

Relying on the power of this grace, I am like a tiger carrying a mountain or a dragon finding water; never abandoning him in thought after thought, never parting from him at every step—this is Samādhi.

From the "Chapter on the Vows of Samantabhadra": If one wishes to accomplish the gateway to the merits of the Tathāgatas, one should cultivate ten kinds of vast vows and practices.

Fourth, repentance of karmic obstructions; fifth, rejoicing in merit; sixth, requesting the turning of the wheel of Dharma;
seventh, requesting the Buddhas to remain in the world; eighth, constantly following and learning from the Buddhas; ninth, always acting in accordance with sentient beings;

The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* is not recorded here in its entirety; rather, following the visualization methods elucidated by Great Master Ciyun, I shall set forth their general outline.

Those who wish to practice the visualization for rebirth should go to a single location, sit upright in the lotus posture on a rope bed facing west, with the crown of the head and the spine aligned, neither leaning back nor hunching forward.
They should regulate the breath and stabilize the mind. This is the visualization to be practiced.
The Gate: Briefly, two methods are shown; one should follow what is appropriate for oneself, as it is not necessary to employ both. The first is the Universal Contemplation (*sāmānyālambana*).
One should imagine that the merit cultivated at this very moment will result in rebirth in the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).

Immediately, one should give rise to the thought of being born there, visualizing oneself sitting in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*) within a lotus flower. One should form the visualization of the flower closing and then the flower opening. At the moment the flower opens, there appears...
Visualize five hundred colored lights coming to illuminate your body. Form the visualization that your eyes open, and you see the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and their lands.
You then sit before the Buddha and listen to the sublime Dharma, hearing all sounds, each of which proclaims the teachings you wish to hear.
Whatever you hear must accord with the twelve divisions of the scriptures. When forming this visualization, you must be exceedingly firm and steadfast in mind.
Without distraction, the mental image is clear and distinct, as if seen with the eyes. After a long time has passed, one arises.

Second, one directly visualizes the sixteen-foot golden body of Amitābha Buddha seated upon a lotus flower. One focuses single-mindedly on the single mark of the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows.
This tuft is fifteen feet in length, five inches in circumference, and has eight facets on its exterior. The interior of the tuft is hollow, curling to the right in a graceful manner.
It revolves between the eyebrows, pure, brilliant, and transparent beyond description. It illuminates and reflects the golden countenance with distinct clarity.

When forming this visualization, settle the mind and focus the thought, remaining firm and unwavering. Furthermore, one should observe that whatever is seen through these mental images—whether accomplished or not—is entirely due to the causes and conditions of conceptualization;
it possesses no real nature or characteristics. All that exists is empty, being exactly as it is.

It is neither identical nor different, neither vertical nor horizontal, and is inconceivable. When mental activity and thought are stilled, one can achieve the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection.

"If one cultivates merit but does not recite the Buddha's name, when the merit is exhausted, one will sink back into the cycle of rebirth. If one recites the Buddha's name but does not cultivate merit, there will be much suffering and hardship on the path to enlightenment."

print and circulate the scriptures; provide offerings to the Saṃgha. Serve teachers and elders with reverence; construct and repair monasteries. Promote the circulation of wholesome Dharma;
prohibit the slaughter of living beings. Purchase and release captive animals; feed the hungry and clothe those suffering from the cold.

Relieving others of their debts, yielding property out of righteousness, returning lost items, rescuing those suffering from illness and distress,
praying for the averting of calamities, performing rites to deliver deceased souls, mediating disputes, and preserving human life—
reciting sutras and cultivating merit as described above can all assist one in attaining rebirth in the Pure Land. Furthermore, since beginningless time...

*An Exposition on the Two Practices—Exclusive and Miscellaneous—of the Six Patriarchs of the Lotus School* (Tang Dynasty), by Master Shandao: Question:

For what reason do you not instruct [practitioners] to perform meditative visualization (*guan*), but instead directly dispatch them to exclusively recite the Name? Answer: Sentient beings have heavy afflictions (*āvaraṇa*) and their faculties are subtle.

The mind is coarse; consciousness flutters and the spirit soars, making contemplation difficult to achieve. For this reason, the Great Sage, out of compassionate pity, directly exhorted [beings] to single-mindedly recite the Name.
This is precisely because the act of reciting the Name is easy, and thus continuous mindfulness arises immediately.

If one can maintain this continuity from thought to thought, taking the end of life as the limit, then ten will be reborn for every ten, and a hundred for every hundred. Why is this? Because there are no external distracting conditions, and one attains the right [concentration].
Because of mindfulness; because it accords with the original vows of the Buddha; because it does not contradict the teachings; and because it follows the words of the Buddha.
If one abandons single-minded mindfulness to practice mixed karmas, one will rarely attain success—perhaps once or twice in a hundred, or three or four times in a thousand. Why is this?
This arises from being distracted by various conditions and agitated by mental turmoil, thereby losing right mindfulness; from being inconsistent with the Buddha’s original vows;

from contradicting the teachings; from failing to accord with the Buddha’s words; and from a lack of continuity in focused attention. Because the mind lacks continuity, one fails to maintain mindfulness of repaying the Buddha’s kindness.

Thus, although one engages in spiritual practice, it is constantly associated with fame and profit. Consequently, one delights in approaching various distracting conditions, thereby creating self-obstruction.
Because it obstructs the correct practice for others' rebirth [in the Pure Land], I have observed that among the clergy and laity in various regions, their understanding and practice differ;

some are single-minded while others are distracted. If one practices with exclusive devotion, ten out of ten will attain rebirth; yet among those who cultivate a mixture of practices without sincerity, not even one in a thousand succeeds.
I pray that all people will reflect well upon this for themselves: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, you must resolutely discipline your mind and subdue yourself.
Do not let this cease by day or night; make it your life’s end your goal. At the moment the preceding thought ceases, the succeeding thought is immediately born.
For long periods and throughout eternal kalpas, you shall enjoy the bliss of unconditioned dharmas until the attainment of Buddhahood—how joyful this is!
The Method for Right Mindfulness at the Hour of Death (same as above).
When an ordinary person is about to die and wishes to be reborn in the Pure Land, they must not fear death; they should constantly reflect that this body is full of suffering.

Impure and evil karma is entangled in manifold ways. If one can cast off this defiled body and be reborn in a Pure Land, it will be exactly as one desires—like shedding tattered clothes to put on precious garments. Settle both body and mind; do not give rise to attachment or longing.
As soon as one encounters illness, one should immediately contemplate impermanence and wait for death with a single-minded focus.

One must instruct family members and visitors who come before me to recite the Buddha’s name for me; they must not engage in idle, miscellaneous talk regarding the present moment, nor discuss the affairs of the household, such as its strengths and weaknesses.
Furthermore, there is no need for soft words of consolation or prayers for peace and well-being, for these are all empty and vain.

Furthermore, if one is gravely ill and approaching the end of life, one's relatives must not shed tears or wail, nor should they utter sounds of lamentation or distress that would disturb the mind and cause one to lose right mindfulness.
Instead, they should all recite the Buddha’s name together, maintaining this until the breath ceases.

It would be a supreme blessing if those who clearly understand the Pure Land were to come frequently to encourage and exhort the dying person. One who relies upon this method will certainly [attain rebirth].
Rebirth [in the Pure Land] is beyond doubt.
Regarding the "Fourfold Distinction between Chan and Pure Land" (Song Dynasty), Master Yongming said:
"To have Chan but no Pure Land—nine out of ten go astray. When the realm of the dark state manifests, one is instantly carried away by it."
If there is no Chan but there is Pure Land, ten thousand who practice will all go [to rebirth]. Once you have seen Amitābha, why worry about not attaining enlightenment?
If there is both Chan and Pure Land, you are like a tiger with horns; in this life you become a teacher of men, and in the future you become a Buddha or a Patriarch.
Without dhyāna there is no Pure Land; there are only iron beds and copper pillars. Through ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, there is not a single person to rely upon.

Question: The *Contemplation Sūtra* clarifies the sixteen gates of contemplation (*ṣoḍaśa-vipaśyanā-mukha*), all of which involve concentrating the mind to cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and contemplating the Buddha’s marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
Only by clearly and perfectly realizing them can one ascend to the Pure Land. How, then, can those with distracted minds be transformed and go there? Answer:

The scriptural text of the nine grades naturally possesses degrees of elevation and decline; from the highest to the lowest, they are all subsumed within two types of mind: first, the concentrated mind (*ekāgra-citta*), such as when practicing the cultivation of meditative contemplation; [the second is the distracted mind]. Regarding the former...

Regarding the lowest grade of rebirth: one must focus the mind exclusively on reciting the Name, supported by the permeation of various virtues, and through the dedication of merit and the making of vows, attain this lowest grade.
Nevertheless, one must take refuge for the duration of one's life and practice with diligence until death; whether sitting or lying down, one should always face westward.
While performing prostrations on the path, and at the time of reciting the Buddha’s name and making vows, one should be earnest and sincere, free from all distracting thoughts.
As if facing execution, or as if confined in a prison, or pursued by enemies, or beset by water or fire, one should single-mindedly seek salvation,

vowing to escape the wheel of suffering, swiftly realize non-arising (*anutpāda*), extensively deliver all sentient beings, perpetuate and honor the Triple Gem, and vow to repay the four debts of gratitude.
Thank you. Such sincere resolve shall certainly not be in vain.

However, if one’s words do not accord with one’s deeds, if the power of faith is slight, if there is no mind of continuous mindfulness, if there is a disposition toward frequent interruption, and if one is indolent during life yet hopes for rebirth at the moment of death—then, being dragged by karmic obstructions, one will likely find it difficult to encounter a virtuous friend when beset by the winds and fires [of dissolution], and right mindfulness will not remain.
It is accomplished. Why is this? The present moment is the cause, and the time of death is the fruit. The cause must be real so that the fruit is not in vain.
When the sound is harmonious, the echo follows suit; when the form is straight, the shadow is upright.

If one wishes for the ten recitations to be perfected at the moment of death, one need only prepare the bridge in advance by gathering and accumulating merit, dedicating it toward that time. If every thought remains unimpaired, then there will be no cause for concern.
Question: If one sees one's nature and awakens to the Way, one immediately transcends birth and death. What need is there to fix the mind on that Buddha and seek rebirth in another realm?
Answer: A true practitioner should examine themselves. It is like a person drinking water; whether it is cold or warm, they know for themselves.

O virtuous ones, you should observe your own practice and understanding. Have you seen your nature and awakened to the Way? Have you received the prediction of the Tathāgata and succeeded to the position of the Patriarchs? Can you be like a horse... [text ends]
Can you match Minglong Shoufu in his contemplation of unimpeded eloquence and his realization of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*?
Can you match Zhizhe of Tiantai in being proficient in both doctrine and commentary, and in possessing both practice and understanding?
These great beings all clearly bestowed their teachings and earnestly exhorted rebirth [in the Pure Land]. Surely they would never have misled others or themselves.

Moreover, the Great Hero has praised it with earnest words from his golden mouth; following the examples of the sages of old, we respectfully receive the Buddha’s decree. It is certainly without error.
As for the various accounts of past and present deeds recorded in the *Wǎngshēng zhuàn* (Biographies of Those Who Attained Rebirth), they are numerous and manifest; one should diligently study them.
One should examine this for oneself. Furthermore, one must personally determine whether, at the time of death, when passing from birth to death, one will certainly attain mastery.

One must ascertain whether the heavy obstacles of evil karma from beginningless time will certainly not manifest before one. One must ascertain whether this single retribution-body will certainly be liberated from saṃsāra.

And one must ascertain whether, when traveling among various species within the three miserable realms and evil paths, one will certainly be free from suffering and affliction, moving with sovereign ease. Heaven...
"O Superior One, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, can you entrust yourself wherever you wish without any obstruction?

If you have attained clear and confident realization, what could be more excellent than this? If you have not yet done so, do not allow momentary pride to lead to eternal sinking and delusion, whereby you lose your own benefit of goodness;
whom else will you blame then? Alas, how tragic! What lamentation can avail now?"

Exhorting others to resolve their minds [for rebirth], with a verse and preface by Master Cizhao on those who practice *nianfo*:
"If one does not resolve the mind to seek birth in the Pure Land, one is merely burying one's head while passing the days, thereby losing the opportunity for spiritual benefit for oneself.
Generally, in practicing *nianfo*, one must first resolve the mind; if one wishes to transcend birth and death and attain rebirth in the Pure Land, one must..."
Let the Great Vow be your primary intention. You must constantly practice mindfulness of the Buddha. Morning and evening, single-mindedly prostrate to Amitābha as if attending upon a sovereign.
Do not let these two times pass; as days go by, you will draw closer. When mind and mouth are in resonance with the Buddha, you are not far from him.
Recite the name with the mouth and contemplate it with the mind; aspire to see the Buddha and make profound, earnest vows, maintaining firm faith without doubt.
As days and years pass and your practice becomes mature, samādhi will naturally be accomplished. At the time of death, Amitābha will welcome you, and the Pure Land will appear before you.
Furthermore, may you, within this present life, constantly encounter virtuous friends and never meet teachers of false views, remaining free from delusion.
My mind does not give rise to indolence. Thus recollecting the Buddha with deep faith and making vows—this is the non-deficiency of the three:

faith, practice, and vow. Seeing the Buddha at the moment of death is not something that comes from without; it is entirely the manifestation of one's own mind. It is like a seed in the earth that sprouts when spring arrives;
how could this be something that comes from without? It all emerges from the earth itself. The practice of the present is likewise so.
Thus, when one’s mindfulness, faith, and aspiration for the Buddha are stored within the ground of the eight consciousnesses, they will manifest at the time of death.
That Amitābha and the Pure Land are not something that comes from without; they all emerge from one's own mind. A verse says:
All phenomena arise from the mind; all phenomena cease within the mind. Thus has the Buddha, the Great Śramaṇa, constantly taught.
If one upholds the precepts but lacks faith and aspiration, they shall not be born in the Pure Land, but will only obtain the blessings of humans and devas.
When these blessings are exhausted, they undergo saṃsāra, revolving through it with difficulty finding liberation.
Reading sutras without the eye of wisdom, one does not understand the Buddha’s profound intent;
though one may attain intelligence in future lives, a distracted mind makes liberation difficult. It is better to practice mindfulness of the Buddha:
in this life, free from fame and profit, even if one does not sit or walk in formal meditation, through the power of making vows and maintaining the precepts, one is Amitābha himself.
Dedicating merit to be born in the Land of Bliss— if one practices in this way, even among a thousand, not one shall fail.
Thus spoke the golden mouth of Śākyamuni; Amitābha himself will embrace them. All Buddhas will protect and remember them, and all devas will guard them well.
Upon seeing such a person who practices mindfulness of the Buddha, they are not far from the Buddha.
One should sit at the site of enlightenment and turn the great wheel of Dharma, universally delivering boundless multitudes.
Like a woman from a poor household who carries in her womb a Wheel-Turning King, whom the various devas constantly protect,
yet the poor woman herself does not know that there is a noble son within her womb— so it is with this person who practices mindfulness of the Buddha.
Their intention is likewise thus: they remember the Buddha and constantly think of him, yet they do not know that before long they shall attain Buddhahood.
Protected by all the Buddhas, such persons remain unaware that they shall be born in the Pure Land.
Instead, they expect to return to a future life, to be born once again among humans—just like a poor person’s household.
Within the earth there are hidden treasures, Which treasure deities constantly guard;

They ensure that nothing is lost, yet the poor man knows not of them. Though a precious treasury exists within his own home, Day after day he seeks wages as a hired laborer to provide for his food and clothing.
The person who now practices mindfulness of the Buddha Is of exactly the same mind.
Those who do not know that the person who recites the Buddha’s name is fully endowed with the *tathāgatagarbha*,
yet say of themselves that they have no share in it and instead seek rebirth among humans, are like those in a household of sick people who possess a truly wondrous medicine but,
being ignorant of the nature of that wondrous medicine, cannot cure their own illness, even as they lie day after day by their bedside.
Though suffering immeasurable pain, this person who now recollects the Buddha likewise possesses such a mind;
unaware of the mind that recollects the Buddha, they are able to extinguish greed, hatred, and delusion.
They are able to act as a great King of Physicians and a great Treasury of Jewels, benefiting and delivering all people, and acting as a Great Dharma King.
Protecting all sentient beings, yet regarding them as mere ordinary folk; unable to be born in the Pure Land, they merely observe the precepts for themselves.
Wishing to become human in future lives, they practice the path further through successive rebirths before finally being able to be born in that land.
Many who cultivate the path constantly speak in this way.
Not praising the vows of Amitābha, And not harmonizing with the Pure Land sutras, The mind is shrouded by the barrier of false views;
Ultimately, it is difficult to escape. This is not the obstacle of others, But entirely the obstacle of one's own mind.
If you do not attain birth in this life, One missed opportunity is a hundred missed opportunities. I exhort you, O practitioner!
Believe me, as the Tathāgata has said: the Buddha never speaks words that are not true. How could these be empty or deceptive?
You should simply exert yourself with diligence and seek the Pure Land with a single mind.
Just as fire fueled by wind requires little effort to spread, if you possess the heart of mindfulness of the Buddha and turn your vows toward transcending the triple world, you shall surely succeed.
Meeting with jewels, one does not take them; Encountering food, one suffers from long-term hunger.
Alas! Great man, you do not perceive the true meaning. I now offer this brief exhortation and praise:
Pass it on from person to person, and for my sake spread it widely. Act as an emissary of the Tathāgata; You are truly a child of the Buddhas.
Truly repay the Buddha’s grace; may all universally practice as taught. May we together be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Regarding the cultivation of the Pure Land, Master Huxi [Zhaozhou] said:
"Those who cultivate the Pure Land must truly strive to confront birth and death; it is not a matter of merely speaking of it and then leaving it at that."
You must contemplate how impermanence is swift; time does not wait for anyone. You must take this as a single, unified matter before you can succeed.
If you advance half-heartedly and retreat half-heartedly, or if you waver between faith and doubt, how could such a state ever suffice? How then could you escape the cycle of saṃsāra?
If you can truly believe this, then from this very day forward, arouse great courage and great diligence.
Do not concern yourself with whether you understand or not, nor whether you have seen your nature or not; simply hold fast to the single phrase "Namu Amida Butsu.
Be like one leaning against Mount Sumeru, unshakable and immovable. Concentrate your mind and unify your will.

In mind, one may engage in recollective thought, contemplative thought, mindfulness, or ten-fold mindfulness; or practice silent recitation, focused recitation, bound mindfulness, or reverent recitation.

Let the mind dwell upon this very object; constantly remember and constantly recite. Recite at dawn and recite at dusk; recite while walking and recite while sitting. Let the mind’s recitation not pass in vain;
let the recitation of the Buddha never depart from the heart. Day after day, moment after moment, do not let it go; maintain it with continuous and subtle intimacy.
It is secret. Like a hen brooding her eggs, one must constantly ensure that the warmth remains uninterrupted; this is precisely what is meant by the continuous succession of pure mindfulness.
When further augmented by the illumination of wisdom, one realizes that the Pure Land is none other than one's own mind. This is the method of cultivation for those of superior intelligence.

If one can maintain this with such stability, act as its master, and rely upon it with such firmness, then even when the conditions of suffering and pleasure, or adversity and favor, manifest before them, [they remain unmoved].

This is the mindfulness of Amitābha Buddha. Without a single thought of wavering mind, without a single thought of regressive indolence, and without a single thought of distracted conceptualization, one proceeds until the end of life, never again entertaining other thoughts, with the firm resolve to be born in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
If one can indeed apply oneself with such diligence, then the ignorance accumulated over kalpas and the karmic obstructions of birth and death will naturally vanish.

Upon death, the habitual defilements of worldly toil will naturally be purified and exhausted without remainder. One will personally behold Amitābha Buddha without departing from one's original mindfulness.
When merit is perfected and practice fulfilled, supported by the power of vows, one will certainly be reborn in the highest grade at the moment of death.

Focusing the mind on a single thought is the same as the practice of the High Truths through faith; it is the definitive requirement for being born in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss. Focus the mind on a single thought.
Holding the single phrase "Amitābha Buddha"—this single thought alone is my original teacher;
this single thought alone is the transformation Buddha; this single thought alone is the valiant general who shatters hell;
this single thought alone is the precious sword that slays all evils; this single thought alone is the bright lamp that opens up the darkness. This single thought alone...
This single thought is the great ship for crossing the ocean of suffering. This single thought is the excellent remedy for escaping birth and death.
This single thought is the path for exiting the triple world. This single thought is the Amitābha of one's own nature.
This single thought reaches the Pure Land of Mind-Only. It is simply a matter of remembering this one phrase: "Amitābha Buddha."
Be mindful. Do not let it be lost. Let mindfulness be ever-present in every thought-moment; let it never depart from the mind. Be mindful thus when there is nothing to do;
be mindful thus when there is something to do. Be mindful thus in times of peace and joy; be mindful thus in times of illness and suffering.
Be mindful thus at birth; be mindful thus at death. When this single thought is clear and undeluded in this way, what further need is there?
Question: Is one seeking the path home?
[The Master] reveals that Great Master Lianchi taught that deluded thoughts are the disease and mindfulness of the Buddha is the medicine.
A chronic illness cannot be cured by a single dose; accumulated delusions cannot be resolved in a moment.

The principle is one: that mindfulness can eliminate them. Do not concern yourself with the proliferation of deluded thoughts; it is simply a matter of being diligent and precise in reciting the Buddha’s name.
With every syllable distinct and every phrase continuous, maintaining this with all your might, you will finally have a portion of progress.
As it is said, through true accumulation and long-term effort, there comes a sudden, expansive realization—like grinding a pestle into a needle, or smelting iron into copper.
This is certainly not false. There are many gateways to the Way, but this one alone is the most direct shortcut. It must not be neglected;
it must not be neglected.
This Way is most profound and most subtle, yet it is also most concise and most easy. Because it is so concise and easy, those of lofty intelligence tend to neglect it.
Indeed, birth and death do not depart from a single thought-moment; even all phenomena of the mundane and supramundane worlds do not depart from a single thought-moment.
To now recite the Buddha's name with this very thought-moment—how intimate, immediate, essential, and substantial it is!

If one can penetrate the place where this thought arises, that is the Amitābha of one’s own nature (svabhāva), and that is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West. Even if one does not awaken to it, by riding upon this...

Through the power of mindfulness, you shall be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss; furthermore, you will cut across the stream of birth and death and no longer undergo cyclic existence, until you finally attain great enlightenment.
I pray that you will let go of all external conditions and maintain constant awareness at every thought throughout the twelve periods of the day—this is my highest hope for you.
The ancients taught that one should draw near to a wise teacher and seek out virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Yet, these virtuous friends possess no secret dharma-gates to be transmitted orally or bestowed from mind to mind; rather, simply to untangle people's adhesions and remove their fetters is itself the secret.
Now, merely to uphold the Name with single-mindedness and without distraction—these eight characters are themselves the secret dharma-gate for untangling adhesions and removing fetters.
This is precisely the grand, open road for transcending birth and death. Whether recollecting in the morning or evening, while walking or sitting, let mindfulness continue from moment to moment;
then, samādhi will naturally arise of itself—do not seek it elsewhere.
For those who possess true faith in the Pure Land and have resolved to be reborn there, it matters not whether they have attained awakening or not.

Even for those who follow the "single transmission" and "direct pointing" of Zen but have not yet awakened—though they may devote their days to the practice of *chan*—it does not hinder them from making the vow for rebirth in the Pure Land.
This is because, as long as they have not escaped future existence (*punarbhava*), they will inevitably have a place of birth. This is not a matter of a "stolen mind" or a "deviant path."
Regarding those who have already attained awakening, an ancient said: "Do you suppose that a single awakening is sufficient to place you on equal footing with all Buddhas?

Thus, although Samantabhadra is the eldest son of the Avataṃsaka, and though every dust mote is a Flower Store World (Huāzàng) and every location is a Lotus Land, the *Gongde Xingyuan Pin* (Chapter on the Vows of Conduct) speaks with earnest persistence of rebirth in Sukhāvatī.
If this is so for those who have already awakened, it can be inferred for those who have not yet done so.
Thus it is said.
To alert the assembly:
entering the essential gate of the Path, faith is foremost. Even evil deeds do not succeed without faith; how much more so the case of wholesome deeds?
For example, when a thief in the world is eventually exposed, the government does not fail to punish him with the ultimate penalty.
Yet, even after being released later on, he remains as before and feels no remorse. Why is this? Because he has gained confidence in this particular path;
without investing a single coin of capital, he reaps incalculable profit. Therefore, despite undergoing all manner of suffering and pain, he is determined never to retreat or repent. Now...
When people recite the Buddha's name, they are unwilling to apply themselves with earnest diligence; this is simply because they have not reflected deeply or developed true faith.

It is not that they do not believe in the Pure Land, but even regarding a single phrase spoken by the World-Honored One—that "human life lies between a single inhalation and exhalation"—they fail to take it to heart.
The meaning of this principle is not difficult to explain; you have personally seen it with your own eyes and personally heard it with your own ears through many such precedents.
Now, for you to truly believe these words is already beyond reach.
If you can truly believe these words, then regarding the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation, there is no need for me to exhaust my efforts.
The vital energy (*qi*) has thousands of branches and ten thousand dependencies; once it follows its natural course like water rushing into a ravine, even ten thousand oxen cannot pull it back.
I have observed that when newly initiated students first take a single phrase of the Buddha and place it upon their hearts, their idle thoughts and delusions only become more turbulent and boiling.
They then claim that the practice of *nianfo* (reciting the Buddha’s name) cannot concentrate the mind, failing to realize that this has been so for you throughout immeasurable kalpas.
As for the root cause of birth and death, how can it be severed immediately? Furthermore, the moment when myriad thoughts fly about is precisely the time to apply the practice.
As they scatter, gather them back; as they scatter, gather them back. After a long time, when the practice becomes mature, deluded thoughts will naturally cease to arise.
Moreover, your ability to perceive these deluded thoughts is none other than the Buddha’s own voice. If you do not recite the Buddha’s name...
At that time, the waves surge and flow with great turbulence, ceasing not for even a single moment; how could one possibly be aware of this oneself?
Regarding the recitation of the Buddha's name, there is silent recitation, loud recitation, and *vajra*-recitation. However, loud recitation is too strenuous.
Reciting silently may easily lead to dullness. It is simply a matter of maintaining a continuous and dense flow, with the sound occurring between the lips and teeth;
this is what is called *vajra-japa*. However, one must not be rigidly fixed in this approach. If you feel it is too strenuous, it is permissible to recite silently;

if you feel dullness setting in, it is permissible to recite aloud. Those who practice the recitation of the Buddha's name nowadays are merely striking their hands like fish eggs, following along with their mouths.
If one merely shouts, no benefit will be gained. It is essential that every word leave the mouth and enter the ear, and every sound awaken one's own mind.
For example, if one person is in a deep sleep and another calls out, "So-and-so," the sleeper will immediately wake up.
Therefore, the recitation of the Buddha's name is most effective for gathering the mind.
People today are unwilling to practice mindfulness of the Buddha simply because they look down upon the Western Pure Land.

They do not realize that rebirth in the West is the domain of those with great virtue, great merit, great wisdom, great insight, and who are truly sages and worthies; it is the transformation of this Sahā world into a pure land.
It is not a matter of some minor circumstance. Just look at this city: in a single day and night, how many people die?
Let alone being reborn in the Western Paradise, even among a thousand or ten thousand people, there is not yet one who is reborn in heaven.
As for those who pride themselves on their practice, they achieve nothing more than avoiding a human rebirth in a lower form. Therefore, our World-Honored One’s great compassion—

With compassion, he revealed this Dharma gate; its merit surpasses that of heaven and earth, and his kindness exceeds that of one's own parents. Even grinding one's bones to powder and crushing one's body would not suffice as a repayment.
Thus was it revealed by Great Master Hanshan.
Seeking rebirth in the Pure Land through the recitation of the Buddha’s name is fundamentally intended to resolve the great matter of birth and death.
Nowadays, people only begin to recite the Buddha’s name once they have resolved to end birth and death, merely asserting that the Buddha can bring about this liberation.

However, if one does not understand the root and source of birth and death, toward what exactly is one reciting? If the mind that recites the Buddha’s name cannot sever the roots of birth and death, then it is in vain.
How can one bring an end to birth and death? What is the root and trunk of birth and death? An ancient said: "If karma is not heavy, one will not be born in Saha;
if craving is not severed, one will not be born in the Pure Land. From this we know that craving is the very root and trunk of birth and death.
Tracing back this root of craving, it was not acquired in this present life, nor was it acquired in one, two, three, or four lifetimes. It has existed since time without beginning...

From the very beginning, throughout life after life and birth after birth as we have cast off one body and taken up another, when has there ever been a single thought-moment free from this root of craving?
This seed of craving has accumulated over kalpas until it is profound and deep; therefore, birth and death are endless.
Today, you have only just resolved to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, yet you merely hope for a void rebirth in the Western Land, remaining ignorant even of the root of birth and death itself.

How could there ever have been a single thought that severed attachment? Since one does not know the root of birth and death, one recites the Buddha’s name on one side while the root of birth and death continues to grow unchecked.
Reciting the Buddha’s name in this manner has no relation whatsoever to birth and death;
when the time comes for the end of life, one sees only the root of craving for birth and death manifest before one. Only then does one realize that the Buddha has provided no benefit at all.
It is too late to regret this. Therefore, I exhort those who practice nianfo today: first, you must recognize that craving is the root of birth and death;
as you recite the Buddha's name now, you must sever this root of craving in every thought-moment. This applies even to those currently practicing nianfo at home amidst the affairs of daily life.
Among the children, grandchildren, family affairs, and property seen with the eyes, there is not a single thing that is not loved;
it is as if one's entire body were within a pit of fire. Love is the sovereign master, while the recitation of the Buddha’s name is merely a superficial veneer.
For instance, when the sentiments for one's children and wife manifest before you, turn the light back and look: can this single utterance of "Buddha" truly withstand such love?
"Ma! Indeed, can you sever this craving? If you cannot sever this craving, how will you ultimately bring an end to birth and death?
Therefore, I exhort those who practice Buddha-recitation: first, you must have a sense of urgency regarding birth and death; you must have a sense of urgency in severing the mind of birth and death;
you must, moment after moment, cut through the very roots of birth and death. Then, every thought-moment will be the realization of the end of birth and death."

It is a matter of timing. If one’s every thought-moment is thus sincere and earnest, as if every stroke of the blade drew blood, then if one does not transcend birth and death, the Buddhas would be guilty of speaking falsehoods.
The foremost requirement for cultivation is a sense of urgency regarding birth and death; if one lacks such urgency regarding birth and death, how can one dare claim to be reciting the Buddha’s name?
It forms a continuous mass. Furthermore, since immeasurable kalpas ago, sentient beings have harbored deluded thoughts in every moment, their emotional faculties firmly shrouded.

Even though they have now been born into this world, how many times have they ever felt a single thought of genuine anguish regarding birth and death? Day after day, moment after moment, they follow their emotions without ever reflecting inwardly.
Now, you wish to sever the cycle of birth and death accumulated over many kalpas with a superficial and floating faith—this is what is called "trying to save [a drowning man] with a drop of water."
How could there be such a principle as a fire built from accumulated firewood?

If you are truly earnest about birth and death, and if every thought is like saving your head from being set on fire, you must fear that once you lose this human body, it will be difficult to regain it for hundreds of kalpas.

Therefore, bite down firmly on this single sound of "Buddha," resolutely overcoming delusive thoughts so that they manifest before you at every moment in all places, without being obstructed by them. Thus...

Exert yourself with diligent and earnest effort; after a long time, through mastery, you will naturally attain resonance. Without even seeking to form a continuous state of mind, it will spontaneously become one.
You must be courageous and resolute; do not hesitate any longer.
Whenever you practice mindfulness of the Buddha, first set aside all the distracted and discursive thoughts within your breast until there is nothing further to set aside.
Then, single-mindedly bring forth the phrase "Amitābha Buddha," making it vivid and distinct, uninterrupted in the mind.
It should be like beads strung on a thread, or like the nocks of arrows fitted together, with not even a hair’s breadth of space between them.

By thus applying effort and relying steadfastly, one will not be led astray or distracted by external conditions in any situation. Whether in daily activities or stillness, movement or rest, there will be no confusion or disorder;
even in dreams, it will be as in waking. When the time of death arrives, one’s mind will remain single-minded and undisturbed.
This is precisely the time for transcending birth into the Pure Land.
Aside from the two daily periods of ritual practice, one should simply keep the single phrase "Namo Amitābha Buddha" across one's chest at all times.
Keep it in mind at all times; let not the heart be obscured. Cease all contemplation of worldly affairs and take this single phrase of the Buddha as your very life-root.
Clench your teeth with determination and never relinquish it.

Whether eating, drinking, rising, resting, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, this one sound of the Buddha must be ever-present before you. Should you encounter adversity or favor, joy or anger, or any form of affliction...

When the mind is unsettled by the objects of affliction, take up the single phrase "Buddha" and apply it with forceful pressure; immediately, you will see that the afflictions are extinguished on the spot.

Since every moment of affliction is the root of the suffering of birth and death, to extinguish these afflictions through mindfulness of the Buddha is precisely where the Buddha delivers one from the suffering of birth and death.
If mindfulness of the Buddha can eliminate afflictions, then one may proceed.
To thoroughly understand birth and death, there is no other method than this:

if you can maintain mastery over your afflictions while reciting the Buddha’s name, you will maintain mastery even within dreams. If you maintain mastery within dreams, you will maintain mastery amidst the suffering of illness.
If you maintain mastery amidst the suffering of illness, then at the moment of death, you will know how to depart.
It is settled. This matter is not difficult to practice; it simply requires that one’s single thought be intensely focused on birth and death.

Relying solely and steadfastly upon the single sound of the Buddha’s name, do not seek or contemplate anything else. After a long time, through constant cultivation and mastery, you will naturally attain great peace and joy and achieve great benefit.
Regarding the teaching of the *nianfo* (Buddha-remembrance) method, Master Ouyi’s *Nianfo Men* states:
"There is nothing particularly extraordinary about it; it simply takes deep faith and diligent practice as its essentials. Yunqi said:
"A single phrase of 'Amitābha Buddha' encompasses the Eight Teachings and perfectly subsumes the Five Schools. It is a pity that people today [regard] *nianfo*..."
They regard it as a trivial matter, the practice of foolish men and women. Because their faith is not deep, their practice is likewise insincere;

they spend their days in idle indolence, failing to achieve any pure merit. Even if they employ clever expedients, they invariably take the investigation of the word "Who" (*shui*) as the ultimate goal.
Little do they realize that the present mind capable of recitation is, by its very nature, free from fault and transcends all duality. It is...

When the mental application (*manasikāra*) of discursive thought has been eliminated and severed, the Buddha who is presently being recollected is, from the very beginning, transcendent of the emotional mind and free from conceptual calculation.
What need is there to laboriously discuss the subtle or discourse on the profound? It is simply a matter of valuing the ability to believe and maintaining a steady state. Recite directly:

whether ten thousand times a day and night, or five thousand or three thousand, take it as the standard that they must be performed with certainty and without omission. Vow that for the remainder of this life, you shall never change.
[This is] a correction. If one were not to attain rebirth there, the Buddhas of the three periods would be guilty of speaking falsehoods.
Once rebirth is attained, there is forever no falling back; all manner of Dharma gates will manifest before one. One must strictly avoid being "Zhang San" today and "Li Si" tomorrow.

If you encounter those of the Teachings (Dōgyō), do not merely seek out phrases or extract individual characters; if you encounter those of the Zen School (Shūmon), do not merely think of investigating or questioning.

Answer: When encountering a person who upholds the Vinaya, one further contemplates donning the robes and using the alms bowl; yet, in doing so, every single point remains unresolved and every detail remains unclear.

How could one know that the mastery of reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha, the ultimate teachings and principles of the Tripiṭaka and the Twelve Divisions of the Canon, and even the pivotal mechanisms of the seventeen hundred koans, are all contained within this? The three thousand codes of dignified conduct are likewise therein.
The eighty thousand subtle practices and the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*) are also contained within this.

To truly practice the mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) while letting go of the body, mind, and world is itself great generosity (*dāna*). To truly practice the mindfulness of the Buddha without again giving rise to greed, anger, or delusion is itself great ethical discipline (*śīla*).

To truly practice the mindfulness of the Buddha without calculating right and wrong or self and others is itself great patience (*kṣānti*). To truly practice the mindfulness of the Buddha without even the slightest...

To be free from interruption and admixture is great diligence; to truly be able to practice nianfo (mindfulness of the Buddha) without further chasing after delusive thoughts is great meditative concentration;
to truly be able to practice nianfo without being confused by other paths is great wisdom. Try examining yourself.
If body, mind, and the world have not yet been let go; if thoughts of greed, anger, and ignorance still arise spontaneously;

if notions of right and wrong, or self and others, still linger in the heart; if interruptions and intermingling have not yet been entirely eliminated; if delusive thoughts still pursue their objects without ceasing forever;
and if various external diversions can still distract the will—then this is not true mindfulness of the Buddha. One must reach the state of single-mindedness.
Do not allow the boundaries of the mind to become confused, nor is there any other expedient.

When first beginning, you must clearly use a prayer bead to keep track and establish a fixed course of practice that is never lacking. After a long time, through mastery, it will become natural even without conscious recollection;
only then may you count or not count as you please. If, at the outset, you insist on speaking of "fine words" or strive for non-attachment to forms, [you will fail].
One must study to achieve perfect integration and sovereign freedom. This failure is always due to a lack of deep faith and a lack of diligent practice.
Even if you can expound the twelve divisions of the teachings and deliver seventeen hundred turning phrases, these are all matters pertaining to the shore of birth and death;
they will certainly be of no use at the moment of death. Take heed!
The practice of mindfulness of the Buddha values nothing more than genuine faith. First, one must believe that I am a Buddha-to-be, while Amitābha is a Buddha already perfected;

their essence is non-dual. Next, one must believe that this Sahā world is suffering and that the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang) is a place to which one may return, thereby cultivating a fervent longing for the latter and a revulsion toward the former.
Finally, one must believe that every movement and action in the present moment can be turned toward the West.
Furthermore, if one does not dedicate [the merit], even superior-grade goodness will not lead to rebirth there.

However, if one knows how to dedicate, even if one has mistakenly committed evil deeds, by swiftly severing the continuity of such thoughts and giving rise to earnest and profound repentance, the power of that repentance can also enable one to attain rebirth there.
How much more so for those who maintain the precepts and cultivate merit through various superior deeds—how could these not suffice to adorn a pure land?

It is simply because the power of their faith is not deep that their superior deeds sink into the realm of outflows (*āsrava*). Furthermore, to wish to abandon this and seek another path is a grave error indeed.
One need only increase one's true faith; there is no need to alter any of one’s current practices.

For over thirty years, he guided and transformed others according to their capacities, directing them toward the Western Pure Land. Following [him]...

[The monk] said, "I am still speaking falsely. Master Wen said, "Disciple, I am truly not speaking falsely. Why do you, Venerable Sir, say that I am speaking falsely?
The one dressed as a monk said, "All sentient beings take the false for the true and cling to the provisional as real;

therefore, they undergo the cycle of rebirth. If there were a wise person who knew this to be empty and illusory, there would be no such cycling. Do not delude yourself and lose your original nature."
"True Mind. You should know that true mind is no-mind; true knowledge is no-knowledge. Discursive awareness is a demon;
the Buddha has neither knowledge nor awareness. You should believe and accept this; do not harbor doubts. Upon hearing these words, Master Wen attained enlightenment.
He further said, "What the Venerable Elder has spoken is truly the Buddha-dharma; it is inconceivable. I ask the Venerable Elder: since you yourself [are Amitābha Buddha]..."
[The three men] came from within the city. "Have you ever seen Amitābha Buddha? One man on the left replied, "I have told you before, but you would never believe me;
you must see him for yourself. The three rose together and each struck the crown of Master Wen’s head once, then spoke this verse:
"One should be diligent and energetic, cultivating all pure deeds. When the cause is deep, [the result is vast]."
"Regarding this fruit, be careful not to give rise to doubt. It is further said: 'All phenomena arise from the mind; all phenomena cease within the mind. The nature of the mind is originally empty;
grasping and rejecting are unattainable. It is also said: 'The arising of the Buddha-mind and its phenomena are like objects in a dream, like the samādhi of illusion.
You have already understood a small portion of this. When the verse ended, he suddenly saw Maniṅliang (Mañjuśrī) standing there, solemn and majestic."
With dignified deportment, he prostrated himself before the three men. The three men then soared into the air and departed toward the west.

From the sky, the sounds of music were resonant and clear, and the voice of the Buddha rang out brightly. Ningliang again prostrated three times toward Master Wen and said, "I have received your instruction to arouse the aspiration for enlightenment."
I take refuge in the Triple Gem and diligently cultivate pure deeds; having now been born in the Pure Land, I have attained great peace and happiness.

Therefore, I seek the Bodhisattva to come and expound the wondrous Dharma, so as to repay his profound kindness. Furthermore, I prostrated three times toward Master Wen, joined my palms in mindfulness of the Buddha, and departed toward the west.
Just as the morning bell suddenly rang out, I started awake. At dawn, I recorded this as the "Account of a Dream."
I, [the Master], consider that this dream has three causes and conditions:

first, to enable those who cultivate pure practices to understand the primary meaning—that there is mindfulness without thinking and birth without arising—and so that they do not linger midway but proceed directly to the precious abode;

second, to cause those of reckless Chan to sever the views of external paths and realize that there is the single gate of the Pure Land, thereby generating the aspiration for supreme bodhi and practicing according to the nature of illusion.
Samādhi. The gallop of the three horses passes away; once gone, it is profound and distant. Even if one enters the womb of a lotus, who can hear or see?
To briefly communicate this news, the public record is clear and manifest: these are the causes and these are the effects, following each other like a shadow follows a form. How could they be denied?
I have recorded these events to serve as the eyes for the Lotus School. Thus it is said.
After my wife, Lady Fei, had passed away, the disciple of the Jade Altar, Huang Jingfu, sought guidance from the Great Being of the Universal Gate (Guanyin).
The Great Being revealed: "If one can direct the merit with a single thought, the mind shall arrive at the Western Land first; for her cultivation of merit has long been accumulated."
Ultimately, they shall not regress from Bodhi. They will be reborn in the Land of Indolence (*Śithilā*) in their present life, but in the future, they may ascend to the nine grades of rebirth.

Examining the *Bodhisattva-tsa-t'ai ching* (Sutra on the Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb), it says: "Among all sentient beings who have resolved [for enlightenment] and wish to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, they all take pleasure in and become attached to the land of Indolence, and thus cannot advance further.
Yuan Xiaoxiu’s record of Zhonglang’s words states: "The borderland of the West..."
It is named the Land of Indolence (*Sthira*). Those whose faith and understanding are not yet established and whose jewel of the precepts is incomplete are mostly reborn there;

those in the Jade Towers and nearby Halls are all their companions. Although Fei’s power in maintaining the precepts surpassed that of the other two, her wisdom and understanding were inferior, and she was likewise unable to practice with diligence.
Judging the fruit by its cause, it is only natural that she was born in a borderland; let this be discussed in conjunction with the foregoing.
